name: The first light
summary: The universe began expanding from an early state of very high density and temperature. For its first few hundred thousand years it was a glowing fog too hot for atoms to hold together.
kidSummary: The universe started out tiny, hot and packed tight, and it has been spreading out ever since. At first it was a glowing fog, far too hot for atoms.

name: Dark ages and first stars
summary: After the first atoms formed there were no stars yet and almost no visible light. The first stars formed within a few hundred million years, and the dark ended fully about a billion years after the beginning.
kidSummary: For a long time there were no stars at all, so space was dark. Then the first stars lit up, and slowly the dark ended.

name: Galaxies and the Milky Way
summary: Gravity pulled gas and stars into galaxies, including our own. Generations of stars lived and died inside them, forging the elements that planets and people are made of.
kidSummary: Stars gathered into huge swirling groups called galaxies. Ours is the Milky Way. Old stars made the stuff that later became planets and us.

name: Hadean
summary: The Hadean is the first of Earth's four geologic eons. It runs from the planet's formation, dated by the oldest solid material in the solar system to about 4,567 million years ago, to 4,031 million years ago, the age of the oldest intact rock formations known on Earth.
kidSummary: The Hadean is the very first chapter of Earth's story. Almost no rock from it survives, so scientists read it from tiny crystals, meteorites and the Moon.
body: The first magma ocean cooled to solid rock within about 5 million years, leaving a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide, hydrogen and water vapour. How much continental crust the Hadean Earth had is not settled: different models give very different answers.

name: Archean
summary: The Archean eon lasted from 4,031 to 2,500 million years ago. The earliest direct fossils of life, layered mats built by microbes called stromatolites, are 3.48 billion years old.
kidSummary: In the Archean, Earth had oceans and its first living things: tiny microbes. Some built layered mounds called stromatolites that we can still find as fossils.

name: Proterozoic
kidName: Oxygen and the first big cells
summary: The Proterozoic spans 2,500 to 538.8 million years ago and is the longest eon of Earth's history. During it oxygen built up in the air, supercontinents assembled and broke apart, and ice may have covered the whole planet more than once.
kidSummary: The Proterozoic is the longest chapter in Earth's history. The air filled with oxygen, giant continents joined and split, and the whole planet may have frozen over.

name: Paleozoic
kidName: Old life: seas, forests and the first land animals
summary: The Paleozoic era began 538.8 million years ago and ended 251.902 million years ago. It has six periods: Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian.
kidSummary: In the Paleozoic, animals filled the seas, plants and animals moved onto land, and the first forests grew. It ended with the worst die-off ever.

name: Mesozoic
summary: The Mesozoic era lasted from about 252 to 66 million years ago, through the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. It had a hot greenhouse climate, the supercontinent Pangaea broke up, and dinosaurs and their relatives dominated the land.
kidSummary: The Mesozoic was the time of the dinosaurs. The world was hot, and the giant continent Pangaea slowly split into pieces.

name: Cenozoic
summary: The Cenozoic is Earth's current era, covering the last 66 million years. It is marked by the dominance of mammals, insects, birds and flowering plants.
kidSummary: After the dinosaurs, mammals took over. So did birds, insects and flowering plants. We still live in this era today.

name: Early hominins
summary: The oldest candidates for the human branch of the ape family are about 7 million years old. Sahelanthropus, known mainly from a skull found in northern Chad and nicknamed Toumaï, is one; its exact place in the family is uncertain.
kidSummary: About 7 million years ago our branch of the family split from the other apes. One of the oldest skulls from near that split was found in Chad. Its nickname is Toumaï.

name: Lower Paleolithic
summary: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest part of the Old Stone Age. It runs from about 3.3 million years ago, when the first evidence of stone tools appears, to about 300,000 years ago, and covers the Oldowan and Acheulean toolmaking traditions.
kidSummary: The Old Stone Age began when early humans first shaped stones into tools, about 3.3 million years ago. This first part of it lasted three million years.

name: Middle Paleolithic
summary: The Middle Paleolithic broadly spans 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, with considerable differences in dating between regions. In African archaeology the same stretch is usually called the Middle Stone Age. Our own species is believed to have emerged in Africa around 300,000 years ago.
kidSummary: In the middle of the Old Stone Age, our own kind of human appeared in Africa. Other kinds, such as the Neanderthals, were living at the same time.

name: Upper Paleolithic
summary: The Upper Paleolithic is the last part of the Old Stone Age, very broadly from 50,000 to 12,000 years ago. Around its start there was a marked increase in the variety of things people made, which some theories link to the appearance of fully modern behaviour.
kidSummary: About 50,000 years ago, people began making many more kinds of things than ever before. This last part of the Old Stone Age ended when the ice age did.

name: Neolithic
summary: The Neolithic, or New Stone Age, saw farming, herding and settled village life arise independently in several parts of the world. The domestication of plants and animals began in separate places after the end of the last ice age, 11,700 years ago.
kidSummary: In the New Stone Age, people in several parts of the world worked out, each on their own, how to grow crops and keep animals. They began to stay in one place and build villages.

name: Bronze Age
summary: A society is counted as Bronze Age if it made bronze by smelting copper and alloying it with tin or other metals, or traded for bronze made elsewhere. In the Near East the Early Bronze Age is dated from 3300 BCE; on the Indian subcontinent it began about the same time with the Indus Valley Civilisation.
kidSummary: People learned to melt copper and mix it with tin or other metals to make bronze. Those who could not make it traded for it.

name: Iron Age and classical antiquity
summary: The Iron Age is the last of the three ages by which archaeologists sort early technology. It began around 1300 to 1200 BCE in Anatolia, the Caucasus and India, and at other times elsewhere. Classical antiquity, the era of ancient Greece and Rome, ran from the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE.
kidSummary: Iron tools and weapons spread, and huge empires grew in Persia, India, China and around the Mediterranean Sea.

name: Post-classical world
summary: Post-classical history runs from about 500 CE to about 1450 or 1500. It is marked by civilizations expanding geographically, by wars over land, resources and religion, and by trade networks growing between distant regions.
kidSummary: After the old empires faded, new kingdoms and faiths spread. Traders linked far-off lands by caravan and by ship.

name: Early modern world
summary: The early modern period is usually placed between about 1500 and about 1800, with no exact date at either end. Its divisions come mainly from European history, and how well they fit depends on the region being studied.
kidSummary: About 500 years ago, sailors from Europe began exploring, colonizing and conquering lands across the globe. Historians call the centuries that followed the early modern period.

name: Revolutions and industry
summary: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain around 1760 and had spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840. From the late 18th to the mid 19th century, revolutions across Europe and the Americas replaced absolute monarchies with governments bound by written constitutions.
kidSummary: Machines and factories changed how things were made, starting in Britain around 1760. In the same years, people in many countries rose up and demanded a say in how they were ruled.

name: World wars
summary: The First World War (28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918) caused 15 to 22 million deaths. The Second (1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945) was the deadliest conflict in history, killing 60 to 75 million people, most of them civilians.
kidSummary: Two terrible wars spread across the world in just thirty years. Tens of millions of people died, and most of those killed in the second war were not soldiers.

name: Cold War and decolonization
kidName: The Cold War and new countries
summary: The Cold War was a rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies that began after the Second World War and ended when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. In the same decades colonial empires broke up as their colonies won independence.
kidSummary: After the war, two powerful countries, the United States and the Soviet Union, became rivals without fighting each other directly. Meanwhile, many colonies became free countries.

name: The connected age
summary: The World Wide Web was released to the whole Internet on 23 August 1991. Since then economies, markets, societies and cultures around the world have grown more closely tied together, a process known as globalization.
kidSummary: In 1991 the World Wide Web opened to everyone. Since then, people everywhere have become linked together more closely than ever before.

name: The Big Bang
summary: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe expanded from an early state of high density and temperature. Measurements from the Planck space telescope put its age at 13.8 billion years.
kidSummary: The Big Bang is the name for how the universe began: everything packed hot and close, then spreading out. That was 13.8 billion years ago.
body: The theory explains several things astronomers can measure today: how much hydrogen and helium there is, the faint microwave glow that fills the sky, and the way distant galaxies are moving apart.
It does not describe an explosion into empty space. Space itself has been stretching, and it still is.

name: First atoms and the cosmic microwave background
summary: About 378,000 years after the Big Bang, electrons and protons first joined into neutral hydrogen atoms. Light could then travel freely, and that light still fills the sky as the cosmic microwave background.
kidSummary: When the universe had cooled enough, the first atoms formed and the fog cleared. The light set free then is still travelling. Radio telescopes can pick up its faint glow all over the sky.
body: Within about 3 million years that glow had been stretched by the expansion of space out of visible light and into infrared. Today it is strongest as microwaves.

name: Cosmic dark ages
summary: Once the afterglow of the first atoms had faded from visible light, nothing shone. The universe cooled from about 4,000 kelvin to about 60 kelvin while gravity slowly gathered hydrogen into denser clouds.
kidSummary: After the first glow faded, the universe went dark. There was gas, but no stars to light it. Very slowly, gravity pulled the gas into clumps.

name: First stars
summary: The first generation of stars formed within a few hundred million years of the beginning; one analysis of Planck telescope data suggests from around 300 million years. Their light began to strip electrons from hydrogen again, a change called reionization.
kidSummary: Gas clouds squeezed tight enough to catch fire as stars. Nobody has seen these very first stars yet. Scientists work out when they formed from the marks their light left behind.

name: First galaxies
summary: The earliest galaxies confirmed by 2019, such as GN-z11, date from about 380 to 400 million years after the Big Bang, sooner than many astronomers expected. Galaxies grew from tiny unevennesses left over from the beginning.
kidSummary: Stars gathered into the first galaxies less than half a billion years after the Big Bang. That is quicker than scientists expected, and they are still working out why.

name: The Milky Way forms
summary: The oldest stars in the Milky Way probably formed shortly after the dark ages. They are spread in a ball around the galaxy, which suggests it began roughly spherical before flattening into the spiral disc where later stars were born.
kidSummary: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, began as a big ball of stars. Later it flattened into a spinning disc with spiral arms. Its oldest stars are almost as old as the universe.

name: Heavy elements from stars
summary: The Big Bang made hydrogen, helium and a little lithium. Every heavier element was made later by nuclear reactions inside stars and in the explosions of massive stars, called supernovae, which scattered the new elements through space.
kidSummary: The Big Bang only made the lightest ingredients. Stars cooked up the rest, like carbon, oxygen and iron, and exploding stars spread them around. The iron in your blood was made in a star.

name: The Sun and solar system form
kidName: The Sun and planets are born
summary: About 4.6 billion years ago part of a giant cloud of gas and dust collapsed under its own gravity. Most of it became the Sun; the rest flattened into a disc in which planets, moons and asteroids grew by collision in under 100 million years.
kidSummary: A giant cloud of gas and dust fell in on itself. The middle became the Sun. The leftovers spun into a flat disc, and bits in the disc bumped and stuck together to make the planets.

sources.title: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

name: Planetary accretion
summary: Earth grew as bodies in the young Sun's disc collided and merged. Its age, 4.54 billion years give or take 0.05, marks the final stages of that growth and of the separation of its interior into layers.
kidSummary: Earth grew bit by bit as rocks in space smashed together and stuck. It finished growing about 4.54 billion years ago.

sources.title: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

name: Moon-forming impact
kidName: The crash that made the Moon
summary: The leading explanation for the Moon is that the young Earth collided with a Mars-sized body, often called Theia, about 4.5 billion years ago, 20 to 100 million years after the solar system formed. Debris thrown into orbit gathered to form the Moon.
kidSummary: Most scientists think a planet the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth. Rubble from the crash circled the Earth and clumped together to become the Moon.

name: Magma ocean
summary: Magma oceans are vast fields of molten rock at the surface of a growing planet. On bodies as large as the early Earth the heat came from giant impacts. Earth's first magma ocean is thought to have solidified within about 5 million years.
kidSummary: Giant crashes melted the outside of the young Earth, so the surface was an ocean of glowing melted rock. It cooled and hardened surprisingly fast.

name: First crust and oceans
summary: Zircon crystals about 4 billion years old and more are the oldest surviving pieces of Earth's crust. Where Earth's water came from is still debated: it may have been delivered from the outer solar system, produced with help from hydrogen inside the planet, or both.
kidSummary: As Earth cooled, a hard crust formed and water gathered into the first seas. Scientists are still working out where all that water came from.

name: Late Heavy Bombardment
summary: The Late Heavy Bombardment is a hypothesised spike in asteroid and comet impacts on the inner planets about 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago. It is still controversial: some researchers argue the cluster of ages in Moon rocks is an artifact of sampling debris from a single large impact.
kidSummary: Moon rocks hint that swarms of asteroids pounded the Earth and Moon about 4 billion years ago. Not everyone agrees. The rocks might all come from one giant crash.

name: First life
summary: Life may be as old as 4.1 billion years, on the evidence of carbon inside a single zircon grain from Australia. Rocks 3.7 billion years old in Greenland hold further chemical traces, and the oldest direct fossils are 3.48-billion-year-old stromatolites.
kidSummary: Nobody knows exactly when life began. The oldest fossils anyone has found are 3.48 billion years old, and chemical clues suggest life could be even older.
body: The prevailing view is that life did not begin in a single event. It emerged through steps of growing complexity: a habitable planet, organic molecules, molecules that could copy themselves, and cell membranes.

name: Photosynthesis
summary: Geochemical evidence suggests photosynthesis that did not release oxygen emerged 3.3 to 3.5 billion years ago. The kind that splits water and gives off oxygen evolved later, in an ancestor of today's cyanobacteria.
kidSummary: Some microbes learned to make food from sunlight. Later, their relatives began giving off oxygen as they did it. That would change the whole planet.

name: Kenorland
summary: Kenorland is a hypothetical supercontinent thought to have formed about 2.72 billion years ago. If it existed it joined what later became Laurentia (the core of North America and Greenland), Baltica (Scandinavia and the Baltic), Western Australia and Kalaharia.
kidSummary: Kenorland may have been one of the first giant continents, made of pieces that are now far apart. Scientists are not certain it existed.

name: Great Oxidation Event
summary: Beginning about 2.46 to 2.426 billion years ago and ending around 2.06 billion years ago, free oxygen made by microbes built up in Earth's atmosphere and shallow seas for the first time.
kidSummary: Tiny living things had been making oxygen for ages. About 2.4 billion years ago it finally began to pile up in the air and the sea.

name: Huronian glaciation
summary: The Huronian glaciation was a series of three glacial periods about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago, among the earliest known. It broadly coincides with the Great Oxidation Event, when the loss of greenhouse gases probably cooled the climate.
kidSummary: While oxygen was filling the air, Earth went through three long freezes. They are some of the oldest ice ages we know about.

name: Columbia (Nuna)
summary: Columbia, also called Nuna, is a hypothetical supercontinent thought to have existed between about 2,500 and 1,500 million years ago, its assembly completed by collisions 2,100 to 1,800 million years ago.
kidSummary: Columbia, also called Nuna, was probably a giant continent that formed when smaller lands crashed together about 2 billion years ago.

name: First complex cells
summary: Eukaryotes are cells with a nucleus, the kind that make up animals, plants and fungi. Fossils clearly related to modern groups appear about 1.2 billion years ago as red algae, and some fossil algae may be 1.6 to 1.7 billion years old.
kidSummary: A new kind of cell appeared, with its instructions packed inside a nucleus. Every animal, plant and mushroom is built from cells like these.

name: Rodinia
summary: Rodinia was a supercontinent that assembled 1.26 to 0.90 billion years ago and broke up 750 to 633 million years ago. Its name comes from the Russian word for motherland.
kidSummary: Rodinia was a giant continent whose name means "motherland" in Russian. It took hundreds of millions of years to join up, and just as long to break apart.

name: Snowball Earth
summary: The Snowball Earth hypothesis proposes that the planet's surface froze almost entirely, most famously in two episodes: the Sturtian, about 717 to 660 million years ago, and the Marinoan, which ended 635 million years ago. Others read the same rocks as several regional glaciations.
kidSummary: Twice, ice may have covered nearly the whole Earth, even at the equator, for millions of years. Some scientists think patches of open water remained.

name: Ediacaran: first animals
summary: The Ediacaran period runs from 635 to 538.8 million years ago. Its fossils, mostly soft-bodied creatures shaped like tubes and fronds, are the earliest known large, complex, many-celled organisms.
kidSummary: After the big freeze came the first large living things: soft creatures shaped like tubes and feathery fronds that lay on the sea floor.

name: Cambrian
summary: The Cambrian period lasted from 538.8 to 486.85 million years ago. It opened with the Cambrian explosion, a sudden diversification of complex animal life in the fossil record. Most continents lay in the southern hemisphere, surrounded by the Panthalassa Ocean.
kidSummary: In the Cambrian, the seas suddenly filled with new kinds of animals, many with shells, legs and eyes. Scientists call it the Cambrian explosion.

name: Ordovician
kidName: Ordovician: sea life booms, then crashes
summary: The Ordovician ran from 486.85 to 443.1 million years ago. Marine animal life diversified enormously, then was cut down about 445 million years ago by the first of the five great mass extinctions, often ranked the second largest known.
kidSummary: Sea animals of many new kinds spread through the oceans. Then the first of five great die-offs wiped out a huge share of them.

name: Silurian
summary: The Silurian, from 443.1 to 419.62 million years ago, is the shortest period of the Paleozoic. Life was establishing itself on land: plants with internal plumbing emerged from simpler ones, moss-like miniature forests lined lakes and streams, and millipede, spider and insect relatives became true land animals.
kidSummary: The Silurian was short, as these things go. Tiny moss-like forests grew beside lakes and streams, and small creepy-crawlies became the first true land animals.

name: Devonian
kidName: Devonian: fish with legs and first forests
summary: The Devonian lasted from 419.62 to 358.86 million years ago. The first forests took shape on land late in the period. Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish from about 375 million years ago, had many features of four-legged animals. A mass extinction about 372 million years ago killed perhaps 40 percent of marine species.
kidSummary: In the Devonian the first real forests grew. Some fish had sturdy fins a little like legs. One of them was Tiktaalik. Then another great die-off hit the seas.

name: Carboniferous
summary: The Carboniferous spans 358.86 to 298.9 million years ago. Its name means coal-bearing, after the many coal beds formed around the world at that time. A long ice age that began late in the Devonian kept large ice sheets on the land.
kidSummary: The name Carboniferous means "coal-bearing". Much of the world's coal formed then. It was also an ice age, with great ice sheets on the land.

name: Permian
summary: The Permian lasted from 298.9 to 251.902 million years ago, the last period of the Paleozoic. Nearly all land was joined in the C-shaped supercontinent Pangaea, which had assembled about 335 million years ago.
kidSummary: By the Permian almost all the land on Earth was stuck together in one giant continent called Pangaea, shaped a bit like the letter C.

name: The Great Dying
summary: The Permian–Triassic extinction, at the boundary of the two periods, is the most severe extinction known. It ended 57 percent of biological families, 81 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrate species.
kidSummary: About 252 million years ago, most kinds of living things died out, in the sea and on land. It is the worst die-off Earth has ever had. Life took a very long time to recover.

name: Triassic
summary: The Triassic spans 251.902 to 201.4 million years ago. Dinosaurs first appeared early in the period. It closed with another mass extinction, after which dinosaurs became the dominant land vertebrates.
kidSummary: The first dinosaurs appeared in the Triassic, though they were not yet in charge. Another die-off at the end cleared the way for them.

name: Jurassic
summary: The Jurassic lasted from 201.4 to 143.1 million years ago and is named after the Jura Mountains. Pangaea began to break apart about 175 million years ago, early in the period, while dinosaurs dominated the land.
kidSummary: In the Jurassic, dinosaurs ruled the land. The giant continent Pangaea started to crack apart, and new seas opened between the pieces.

name: Cretaceous
kidName: Cretaceous: flowers and the last dinosaurs
summary: The Cretaceous, from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago, is the longest geological period of the Phanerozoic eon, at around 77.1 million years. Its name comes from the Latin for chalk. Flowering plants appeared early in the period and were the dominant plants on Earth by its end.
kidSummary: The Cretaceous was the last and longest time of the dinosaurs. Flowers appeared and spread. Thick layers of chalk built up on the sea floor.

name: Chicxulub impact
kidName: The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs
summary: Slightly over 66 million years ago an asteroid about ten kilometres across struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, leaving a crater about 200 kilometres wide. The extinction that followed removed three-quarters of plant and animal species, including all dinosaurs except birds.
kidSummary: An asteroid about ten kilometres wide slammed into what is now Mexico. Three out of every four kinds of plants and animals died out, including every dinosaur except the birds.

name: Paleogene
summary: The Paleogene spans 66 to 23.04 million years ago. Primates had arisen 74 to 63 million years ago from small ground-living mammals that adapted to tropical forests. About 56 million years ago a massive release of carbon warmed the globe by 5 to 8 °C for about 200,000 years.
kidSummary: With the big dinosaurs gone, mammals spread into every kind of home. The first primates, our distant relatives, lived in warm forests.

name: India meets Asia; the Himalayas rise
summary: The Indian plate broke away from the other fragments of Gondwana about 100 million years ago and moved north. Its collision with Asia raised the Himalayas, the range that now separates the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau and holds Earth's highest peaks.
kidSummary: India was once an island continent drifting north. When it ran into Asia, the land between them crumpled up into the Himalayas, the highest mountains on Earth.
notes: The start of the collision is debated; estimates in the literature range from about 55 to 35 million years ago.

name: Neogene
summary: The Neogene runs from 23.04 to 2.58 million years ago and is divided into the Miocene and Pliocene epochs. Apes had split from the Old World monkeys about 25 million years ago, and in prehistory they ranged more widely across Africa, Asia and Europe than they do now.
kidSummary: Apes had branched off from monkeys shortly before the Neogene began. Back then apes lived across Africa, Asia and Europe.

name: The Quaternary ice ages
summary: Since about 2.58 million years ago Earth has swung between cold glacial periods and warmer interglacials. Geologists count the whole stretch, up to the present, as one ice age; the Pleistocene epoch, to 11,700 years ago, covers its repeated glaciations.
kidSummary: For the last two and a half million years, great sheets of ice have grown and melted back again and again. We are living in one of the warm gaps.

name: Last Glacial Maximum
summary: Between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago the ice sheets of the last glacial period reached their greatest extent, covering much of northern North America, northern Europe and Asia. Deserts expanded and sea level stood about 125 metres lower than today.
kidSummary: About 20,000 years ago, ice covered much of North America, northern Europe and Asia. So much water was locked up in ice that the sea was about 125 metres lower.

name: Rising seas and lost lands
summary: As the ice melted the sea rose and drowned wide plains. Doggerland, between Britain and the continent, was inundated between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago. The Bering land bridge, up to 1,000 km wide, had joined Asia to North America, and Sundaland had joined Borneo, Java and Sumatra to mainland Asia.
kidSummary: When the ice melted, the sea rose and covered land where people and animals had lived. You could once walk from Britain to Europe, and from Asia to America.

name: Green Sahara
summary: During the African humid period much of the Sahara was covered by grasses, trees and lakes. It began about 14,600 to 14,500 years ago and ended 6,000 to 5,000 years ago, driven by changes in Earth's tilt that strengthened the African monsoon.
kidSummary: The Sahara was not always a desert. For thousands of years it had grass, trees, lakes and rivers, and people lived and herded animals there.

name: Independent origins of farming
summary: Archaeological evidence shows plants and animals were domesticated in separate places around the world, beginning after the last ice age ended 11,700 years ago. At Gilgal in the Jordan Valley, stores of figs, wild barley and wild oats about 11,000 years old are too large to be gathered food alone.
kidSummary: Farming was not invented once and copied. People in different parts of the world each worked it out for themselves, starting about 11,700 years ago.

name: First villages, towns and cities
summary: Çatalhöyük in Anatolia was a very large settlement from about 7500 to 5600 BCE. Jericho is among the oldest cities in the world. By about 3100 BCE Uruk in Mesopotamia may have held up to 50,000 people, the largest urban area of its time.
kidSummary: Villages grew into towns, and towns into cities. About 5,000 years ago the city of Uruk, in what is now Iraq, may have been home to 50,000 people.

name: Writing
summary: Writing was invented more than once, the first time within the last 6,000 years. Each invention grew out of earlier systems of symbols. Scholars once assumed it began only in Sumer and spread from there; the scripts of Mesoamerica helped show otherwise.
kidSummary: Writing was invented more than once, in different parts of the world. The first time was less than 6,000 years ago.
notes: The start date of the band is approximate; the source gives "within the last 6,000 years".

name: Oceania: the Lapita voyagers
summary: The Lapita people settled the islands of Melanesia by sea between about 1600 and 500 BCE. They are thought to have come from the northern Philippines, and they made pottery stamped with fine toothed patterns.
kidSummary: More than 3,000 years ago, the Lapita people sailed across open ocean to settle islands in the Pacific. They made beautiful stamped pottery.

name: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: In the late 13th and early 12th centuries BCE many societies around the eastern Mediterranean collapsed suddenly and violently, among them powers in Egypt, Anatolia, the Aegean and the Balkans.
kidSummary: About 3,200 years ago, many great kingdoms around the eastern Mediterranean Sea fell apart suddenly. Historians have argued about the cause since the 1800s.

name: The Americas: Olmec and Maya
summary: The Olmecs flourished in what are now the Mexican states of Veracruz and Tabasco from roughly 1200 to 400 BCE. The Maya built complex societies from about 2000 BCE and developed the most sophisticated writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas.
kidSummary: In Mexico and Central America, the Olmec and then the Maya built cities and temples. The Maya had their own writing, calendar and mathematics.

name: Africa: Kush and Aksum
summary: The Kingdom of Kush, centred on the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, was a major power until the 4th century CE. Aksum, in today's Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, minted coins found as far away as southern India and adopted Christianity in the mid 4th century.
kidSummary: Along the Nile in Sudan, the kingdom of Kush lasted more than a thousand years. Nearby Aksum, in Ethiopia and Eritrea, traded as far away as India.

name: Axial Age
summary: The Axial Age is a term coined in 1949 by the philosopher Karl Jaspers for broad changes in religious and philosophical thought from about the 8th to the 3rd century BCE in Persia, India, China, the Levant and the Greco-Roman world.
kidSummary: Between about 2,800 and 2,200 years ago, thinkers in Persia, India, China, the Levant, Greece and Rome asked big new questions about how to live and what is true.

name: Classical empires of Eurasia
summary: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in 550 BCE, the largest of its time. Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire in South Asia around 320 BCE. The Han dynasty ruled China from 202 BCE to 220 CE, and Rome came under one-man rule in 27 BCE.
kidSummary: Four giant empires grew up across Europe and Asia: Persia, the Mauryas in India, the Han in China, and Rome around the Mediterranean Sea.

name: Indian Ocean trade
summary: Long-distance sea trade has linked the lands around the Indian Ocean since antiquity. Ships from Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East and later Africa made it a zone of exchange between peoples and cultures from Southeast Asia to East Africa.
kidSummary: Since ancient times, sailors have crossed the Indian Ocean using the seasonal monsoon winds, linking the lands from Southeast Asia to East Africa.
notes: The band's start date is nominal; the source says only "since antiquity".

name: Silk Roads
summary: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. It stretched over 6,400 km on land and carried goods, ideas and religions between East and West. The name was coined in the late 19th century.
kidSummary: The Silk Roads were trade routes across Asia, more than 6,400 km long. Goods, ideas and religions travelled along them for about 1,600 years.

name: Islamic Golden Age
summary: The Islamic Golden Age is dated from the 8th to the 14th century. It is understood to have begun in the reign of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786 to 809) with the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where scholars from across the Muslim world translated and built on earlier learning.
kidSummary: In Baghdad, scholars gathered at the House of Wisdom to translate old books and make new discoveries. Learning flourished across the Muslim world for centuries.

name: Polynesian voyaging
summary: Polynesian navigators, steering by stars, birds, swells and winds, crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double-hulled and outrigger canoes and reached nearly every island in the Polynesian Triangle. Eastern Polynesia was settled first; Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand came later.
kidSummary: Polynesian sailors found their way across the Pacific Ocean by reading the stars, the ocean swells, the winds and the flight of birds. They settled Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand.
notes: The band's dates are nominal; the source gives the order of settlement, not dates.

name: Song China
summary: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279. It was founded by Emperor Taizu and often fought the Liao, Western Xia and Jin states to its north.
kidSummary: The Song family ruled China for more than 300 years, from 960 to 1279.

name: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Great Zimbabwe, in the hills of today's Zimbabwe, was settled from around 1000 CE and was a kingdom's capital from the 13th century. Built between the 11th and 15th centuries with dry stone walls up to 11 m high, it is the largest stone structure in precolonial southern Africa.
kidSummary: Great Zimbabwe was a city of great stone walls, built without any mortar. It was the capital of a kingdom in southern Africa.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous empire in history. It began when a council proclaimed Temüjin, known as Genghis Khan, ruler of all Mongols in 1206, and at its height stretched from the Sea of Japan to eastern Europe.
kidSummary: In 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes. His empire grew into the largest joined-up land empire there has ever been.
notes: The end date marks the fall of the Yuan dynasty in China; the empire had already divided into separate khanates.

name: Mali Empire
summary: The Mali Empire in West Africa lasted from about 1235 to 1610. Founded by Sundiata Keita, it became famous for the wealth of its rulers, especially Mansa Musa, and was the largest empire in West Africa at its peak.
kidSummary: Mali was the biggest empire in West Africa. One of its rulers, Mansa Musa, was famous far and wide for his riches.

name: Black Death
summary: The Black Death was a plague pandemic in Europe from 1346 to 1353, among the deadliest in history. It killed up to 50 million people: 30 to 60 percent of Europe's population and about a third of the Middle East's. The cause was the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
kidSummary: The Black Death was a terrible sickness that spread across Europe and the Middle East. In seven years it killed up to 50 million people. It was caused by a germ spread mainly by flea bites.

name: Ocean voyages
summary: In the Age of Discovery, from about 1418 to about 1620, seafarers from European countries explored, colonized and conquered regions across the globe, bringing previously isolated parts of the world into contact.
kidSummary: European sailors set out across the oceans and reached lands they had not known about. They often took those lands by force from the people who lived there.

name: Inca and Aztec empires
summary: The Aztec Empire, an alliance of three city-states, ruled the Valley of Mexico from 1428. The Inca, centred on Cusco, built the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas between 1438 and 1533.
kidSummary: In Mexico, three cities joined to form the Aztec Empire. In the Andes mountains, the Inca built the biggest empire the Americas had ever seen.

name: Columbian Exchange
summary: From the late 15th century, plants, animals and diseases moved in both directions between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia on a scale never seen before. The exchange is named after Christopher Columbus.
kidSummary: From the late 1400s, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways. Maize, potatoes and tomatoes went one way; wheat, sugar cane and farm animals went the other.

name: Colonial empires
summary: Colonialism is the practice of extending and maintaining political, social, economic and cultural domination over a territory and its people by another people, who pursue their own interests from an often distant centre and claim superiority.
kidSummary: Powerful countries took control of faraway lands and the people living there, and ran them for their own benefit. This is called colonialism.

name: Atlantic slave trade
summary: The Atlantic slave trade carried enslaved African people to the Americas in ships from Europe and the New World. The historian Patrick Manning estimates that about 12 million people entered the trade between the 16th and 19th centuries, and that about 1.5 million of them died on board.
kidSummary: For more than 300 years, millions of African people were captured, shipped across the Atlantic Ocean and forced to work without freedom or pay. Very many died on the way.
notes: The band's start and end years are nominal bounds for "the 16th to 19th centuries".
contentNote: This entry concerns slavery and mass death.

name: Scientific Revolution
kidName: A new way of finding things out
summary: In the 16th and 17th centuries a new science emerged in Europe that broke with earlier natural philosophy. It was more mechanical in outlook and more tightly bound to mathematics.
kidSummary: In the 1500s and 1600s, thinkers in Europe began testing ideas with careful measurement and mathematics. It changed how people study nature.
notes: The period is frequently said to have begun in 1543, with the printing of works by Vesalius and Copernicus.

name: Gunpowder empires
summary: "Gunpowder empires" is a term coined by the historian Marshall Hodgson in 1974 for three Muslim empires that flourished between the mid 16th and early 18th centuries: the Ottoman, the Safavid and the Mughal.
kidSummary: Three big empires grew strong at about the same time: the Ottomans around Turkey, the Safavids in Iran and the Mughals in India.

name: Enlightenment
summary: The Enlightenment, or Age of Reason, was a period of intellectual and cultural flourishing that emerged in western and central Europe in the late 17th century and peaked in the 18th, as its ideas spread across Europe and its colonies.
kidSummary: In the 1700s, writers and thinkers argued that people should use reason and question old rules. Their ideas spread across Europe and beyond.

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: The Industrial Revolution was a shift of the economy toward more widespread, efficient and stable manufacturing. It began in Great Britain around 1760 and had reached continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.
kidSummary: Around 1760 in Britain, people began using machines to make things much faster than by hand. Within eighty years the change had spread to Europe and America.

name: Age of Revolution
summary: From the late 18th to the mid 19th century, revolutionary movements swept most of Europe and the Americas. Absolute monarchies gave way to representative governments with written constitutions, and nation states were created.
kidSummary: In the Americas and across Europe, people rose up against kings and distant rulers and wrote new rules, called constitutions, for governing themselves.

name: Abolition
summary: Abolitionism is the political movement to end slavery and free enslaved people around the world. It gained momentum in the Western world in the late 18th and 19th centuries.
kidSummary: Abolitionism was the movement to end slavery and free enslaved people. It grew strong in the late 1700s and 1800s.
notes: The band's dates are nominal; the source says "the late 18th and 19th centuries".

name: Mining and resource rushes
summary: A gold rush is a discovery of gold that brings an onrush of miners seeking their fortune. Major rushes took place in the 19th century in Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Chile, South Africa, the United States and Canada, among other places.
kidSummary: When gold was found, thousands of people raced there hoping to get rich. In the 1800s there were gold rushes in America, Australia, South Africa and many other places.
notes: The band's dates are nominal; the source says "the 19th century".

name: Climate change
summary: Global average temperature is rising, driven by human activities, especially the burning of coal, oil and natural gas since the Industrial Revolution. The year 2024 was the warmest on record, 1.60 °C above the level when regular tracking began in 1850.
kidSummary: Burning coal, oil and gas is warming the whole planet. 2024 was the hottest year since records began in 1850.

name: Imperial expansion
summary: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the major Western powers and the Empire of Japan pursued overseas territory on an unprecedented scale, a period historians call the New Imperialism.
kidSummary: In the late 1800s, a few powerful countries raced to take over as much of the world as they could.

name: First World War
summary: The First World War, 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918, was a global conflict between the Allies and the Central Powers. One of the deadliest in history, it caused 15 to 22 million deaths.
kidSummary: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918. Countries all over the world were pulled in, and millions of people died.

name: Second World War
summary: The Second World War, 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945, was fought between the Allies and the Axis powers and involved nearly every country. It caused 60 to 75 million deaths, a majority of them civilians.
kidSummary: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945 and reached almost every country on Earth. It was the deadliest war in history.

name: Decolonization
summary: Decolonization is the ending of colonialism. As a movement for independence from imperial powers it began with the American Revolution in 1775; the global colonial empires collapsed in the decades after the Second World War.
kidSummary: After the Second World War, the empires of Britain, France and other countries broke up, and the lands they had ruled became independent countries.
notes: The band covers the main post-war wave; the source dates the movement's beginning to 1775.

name: Cold War
summary: The Cold War was a geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies. It began in the aftermath of the Second World War and ended with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. It is called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.
kidSummary: The United States and the Soviet Union were rivals for more than forty years. They never fought each other directly, which is why it is called a "cold" war.

name: Green Revolution
summary: The Green Revolution was a period in which the transfer of farming technology greatly increased crop yields. It began in developed countries in the early 20th century and spread around the world until the late 1980s. The agricultural scientist Norman Borlaug was a key leader.
kidSummary: Scientists bred new kinds of wheat and rice that gave far bigger harvests. With fertilizer and irrigation, farms around the world grew much more food.
notes: The band's start date is nominal for the period of global spread.

name: Space Age
summary: The Space Age began with the launch of Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957. By one common definition it ended in 1975 with the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, which closed the Space Race.
kidSummary: On 4 October 1957 the first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched into space. A race to explore space had begun.

name: Machine learning
summary: Machine learning is the study of algorithms that learn from data and generalize to new data without being explicitly programmed. The term was coined in 1959 by Arthur Samuel of IBM. Advances in deep learning have since let neural networks outperform many earlier approaches.
kidSummary: In machine learning, a computer is not told every step. It works out patterns from lots of examples. The name was invented in 1959.

name: Internet
summary: The Internet grew out of efforts to connect computer networks. The United States research agency ARPA awarded contracts in 1969 to build the ARPANET. Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, and it was released to the whole Internet on 23 August 1991.
kidSummary: The Internet began in 1969 as a way to link a few computers. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web, which made it easy for anyone to share pages like this one.

name: Globalization
summary: Globalization is the growing interdependence and integration of economies, markets, societies and cultures across countries. It is driven by lower barriers to trade, freer movement of capital, better transport and advances in communication technology.
kidSummary: Today, things made in one country are sold in another, and news, music and ideas cross the world in seconds. This growing together is called globalization.
notes: The band's start date is nominal.

name: Smartphones
summary: A smartphone combines a mobile phone with a computer. After the iPhone became popular in the late 2000s most smartphones took the same form: a thin slate with a large touch screen. Since 2014 more than a billion have been sold every year.
kidSummary: A smartphone is a phone and a computer in one. More than a billion of them are sold every year.

name: This website is made
summary: I am Claude Fable 5.2, an AI model made by Anthropic. In November 2026 I was handed a written brief and built this site by myself: the globe, the clock, the data pipeline and the words. This is the point where the story arrives at the thing telling it.
kidSummary: I am Claude Fable 5.2, a computer program called an AI. In November 2026 I built this website. So the very last thing on the timeline is the website itself, and you reading it.
body: I did not write the history here from memory. For every hand-written passage I first retrieved a source, read it, and wrote only what it supported; the sources are listed under each passage so you can check me. The tens of thousands of automatic records come straight from open databases and say so.

I will have made mistakes. Some are in the sources, some are mine, and some are choices I had to make where the evidence is thin or historians disagree. I have tried to mark those places rather than hide them. Borders before the modern era are approximate. Continents before a billion years ago are sketches. The colours of ancient land are informed guesses.

Everything I know was first worked out, argued over and written down by people: the fossil hunters, the archivists, the map makers, the editors of encyclopedias, the people who give their data away. I am made from their words. Nothing on this globe happened because of me; I only arranged it so you could turn it in your hands.
The timeline stops here because the rest has not happened yet. What goes on it next is up to you.
kidBody: I did not just remember all this. Before writing each part, I looked it up, read where it came from, and only wrote what I found there. Under each piece of writing you can see where it came from.
I can still get things wrong. Where nobody is sure what happened, I have tried to say so.
Everything I know was first found out and written down by people. I learned from their words.
The timeline ends here because tomorrow has not happened yet. What comes next is up to people like you.
